title: Steel, cars, chips
hook: One product at a time, the US has put national-security tariffs on metals, cars, wood, medicine and chips. Here is where those goods come from.
notes: Tariffs: presidential proclamations under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (19 U.S.C. 1862), Federal Register: steel and aluminium 25% from 12 March 2025 (Proclamations 10895 and 10896, 90 FR 9807 and 9817), 50% from 4 June 2025 (Proclamation 10947, 90 FR 24199; UK 25%), charged on the full value of the product from 6 April 2026, with 25% or 15% on many derivative products (Proclamations 11021, 91 FR 18201, and 11032, 91 FR 34085); cars 25% from 3 April 2025 and parts from 3 May 2025 (Proclamation 10908, 90 FR 14705; Japan, EU and South Korea 15% under deals implemented at 90 FR 44638, 90 FR 46136 and 90 FR 55964); copper 50% from 1 August 2025 (Proclamation 10962, 90 FR 37727); softwood lumber 10%, upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets 25% from 14 October 2025 (Proclamation 10976, 90 FR 48127; increases postponed to 1 January 2027 by Proclamation 11000, 91 FR 1039); medium and heavy trucks and parts 25%, buses 10% from 1 November 2025 (Proclamation 10984, 90 FR 48451); certain advanced computing chips 25% from 15 January 2026 (Proclamation 11002, 91 FR 2443); patented medicines 100% from 31 July 2026 for listed large companies and 29 September 2026 for others, 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland, generics exempt (Proclamation 11020, 91 FR 18183); drones 100% or 25% from 3 September 2026 (Proclamation 11055, 91 FR 53699); polysilicon and solar minimum import prices from 4 December 2026 (Proclamation 11052, 91 FR 51975). Critical minerals (Proclamation 11001) and aircraft (Proclamation 11040) ended in negotiations, not tariffs, as of 13 October 2026. Rates shown are the general rates; deals, US-content rules for Canadian and Mexican goods and many exemptions change what an importer actually pays. Trade: CEPII BACI, version 202601, US imports in 2024 by country of origin, values in US dollars; product groups approximate the legal scope of each tariff, which is defined by detailed US tariff lines (see the dataset note). Pharmaceuticals include generics, and chips include all integrated circuits, so both overstate what the tariffs cover.

scenes.title: The tariffs the court left standing
scenes.text: Section 232, a 1962 law, lets the president restrict imports that threaten national security, after a Commerce Department investigation. Since 2025 it has been used product by product. The goods hit so far cost the US about $610 billion to import in 2024, nearly one dollar in five. Mexico, Canada, Germany and Japan supply the most.

scenes.title: One product at a time
scenes.text: Pick a product. Each tariff has its own date, rate and rules, and each falls on a different set of countries.

options.label: Steel
options.text: Steel: 25% from 12 March 2025, 50% from 4 June 2025 (25% for the UK). Since April 2026 the tariff applies to the full value of goods, not just their steel. Canada (22%), Brazil (15%) and Mexico (10%) supplied most of the $26 billion the US imported in 2024.

options.label: Aluminium
options.text: Aluminium: same dates and rates as steel, 50% since June 2025. Canada, with cheap hydropower for its smelters, supplied 39% of the $29 billion imported in 2024; China came second with 11%.

options.label: Copper
options.text: Copper: 50% from 1 August 2025 on wire, tubes, sheets and other semi-finished copper. Refined copper cathodes, ores and scrap are exempt. Canada supplied 30% of the semi-finished copper the US imported in 2024.

options.label: Cars
options.text: Cars: 25% from 3 April 2025. Japan, the EU and South Korea later negotiated 15%. Cars from Canada and Mexico that meet trade-agreement rules pay only on their non-US parts. Mexico, Japan and South Korea were the top suppliers of $216 billion of cars in 2024.

options.label: Car parts
options.text: Car parts: 25% from 3 May 2025, with the same deals as for cars. Parts that meet North American trade-agreement rules were spared until customs can tax only their non-US content. Mexico supplied 40% of the $91 billion of parts in 2024.

options.label: Trucks
options.text: Trucks: 25% on medium and heavy trucks and their parts, 10% on buses, from 1 November 2025. Three-quarters of the heavy trucks and buses the US imported in 2024 came from Mexico.

options.label: Lumber
options.text: Wood: 10% on softwood lumber and 25% on upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets from 14 October 2025. Canada supplied almost three-quarters of the softwood lumber the US imported in 2024.

options.label: Medicines
options.text: Medicines: 100% on patented drugs and their ingredients, from 31 July 2026 for big listed companies and 29 September 2026 for the rest. The EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland pay 15%; generics are exempt. Ireland, Germany and Switzerland are the largest suppliers.

options.label: Chips
options.text: Chips: 25% from 15 January 2026, but only on certain advanced computing chips, and not when they are used in US data centres, factories or consumer products. Taiwan and Malaysia supplied over half of the $36 billion of chips the US imported in 2024.

scenes.title: Metals: the neighbour pays
scenes.text: The metal tariffs fall hardest on Canada, the largest foreign supplier of steel, aluminium and copper to the US. In 2024 Canada sold the US about $11 billion of aluminium and $6 billion of steel. Canadian steel and aluminium pay the full 50%; the North American trade agreement gives them no discount.

scenes.title: Cars cross the border many times
scenes.text: Car making in North America is one production line spread over three countries; parts can cross the border several times before a car is finished. Mexico is the largest supplier of both cars and parts to the US. That is why cars and parts from Canada and Mexico pay the 25% only on their non-US content.

scenes.title: Medicine from Europe
scenes.text: Three-quarters of the medicines the US imports come from Europe, led by Ireland, where many US drug companies run large factories, drawn partly by low taxes. The new drug tariff starts at 100% but has wide exits: 15% for European and Asian partners with trade deals, and zero for companies that agreed to build US factories and lower US prices.

chart.title: Pharmaceutical products: largest suppliers to the US

scenes.title: The list keeps growing
scenes.text: The chip tariff is narrow for now, but the proclamation warns of broader ones if talks fail; Taiwan and Malaysia would feel them first. In 2026 the list also grew to drones (100% from September) and solar-grade polysilicon (minimum prices from December). The Supreme Court's ruling against the emergency tariffs left every Section 232 tariff in place.
